title: Wire size: current, voltage drop and AWG to mm²
summary: Tables for picking copper wire: safe current by size, AWG to metric conversion, resistance, and how long a 12 V run can be before voltage drop wastes power. Pick the thicker of the size for heat and the size for voltage drop.

steps.text: Work out the current: amps = watts ÷ volts.
Measure the run: the one-way distance from battery to load, in metres.
Find the smallest wire whose safe current (table 1) is above your fuse rating.
Find the smallest wire that keeps voltage drop at 3% or less over your run (table 3). For 24 V double the lengths; for 48 V multiply by 4.
Use whichever of the two is thicker. Fuse the wire to protect it (see skill_dc_wiring).
Unmarked wire: strip a little and measure the bare copper diameter, or count strands and estimate the area. Compare with table 1.

notes:
## Table 1: copper wire sizes

Safe current is conservative: a wire in a bundle, in a wall or in a cable, with ordinary PVC insulation. A single wire in open air with heat-rated insulation can carry more (up to roughly 1.5–2 times for thick cable), which is why some charts show bigger numbers. For 12 V and 24 V work, voltage drop usually limits you first.

| AWG | Area (mm²) | Metric size that can replace it | Bare diameter (mm) | Resistance (ohms per km) | Safe current (A) | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 22 | 0.33 | 0.5 mm² | 0.64 | 53 | 3 | Signals, sensors, single LEDs |
| 20 | 0.52 | 0.75 mm² | 0.81 | 33 | 5 | Small fans, USB leads |
| 18 | 0.82 | 1.0 mm² | 1.02 | 21 | 7 | Lamp cord, small 12 V loads |
| 16 | 1.31 | 1.5 mm² | 1.29 | 13.2 | 10 | Light extension cords, 12 V lighting runs |
| 14 | 2.08 | 2.5 mm² | 1.63 | 8.3 | 15 | Mains 15 A circuits, 12 V pumps and fridges |
| 12 | 3.31 | 4 mm² | 2.05 | 5.2 | 20 | Mains 20 A circuits, solar panel leads |
| 10 | 5.26 | 6 mm² | 2.59 | 3.3 | 30 | Solar arrays, charge controllers |
| 8 | 8.37 | 10 mm² | 3.26 | 2.1 | 40 | Small inverters, battery links |
| 6 | 13.3 | 16 mm² | 4.11 | 1.30 | 55 | Medium inverters, battery links |
| 4 | 21.2 | 25 mm² | 5.19 | 0.82 | 70 | Inverters, bank interconnects |
| 2 | 33.6 | 35 mm² | 6.54 | 0.51 | 95 | Large inverters, starter cables |
| 1/0 | 53.5 | 50–70 mm² | 8.25 | 0.32 | 125 | Large inverters and banks |
| 2/0 | 67.4 | 70 mm² | 9.27 | 0.26 | 145 | Large inverters and banks |
| 4/0 | 107 | 120 mm² | 11.68 | 0.16 | 195 | Very large banks, forklift cables |

Smaller AWG numbers mean thicker wire. Every 3 AWG steps doubles the copper area.

Resistance in ohms per km for copper is about 17.2 ÷ area in mm².

## Table 3: longest one-way run at 12 V for 3% drop (metres)

3% of 12 V is 0.36 V. The current goes out and back, so these lengths are the distance from battery to load.

| Current | 16 AWG | 14 AWG | 12 AWG | 10 AWG | 8 AWG | 6 AWG | 4 AWG | 2 AWG | 1/0 | 2/0 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 5 A | 2.7 | 4.3 | 6.9 | 11 | 17 | 28 | 44 | 70 | 112 | 141 |
| 10 A | 1.4 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 5.5 | 8.7 | 14 | 22 | 35 | 56 | 70 |
| 20 A | 0.7 | 1.1 | 1.7 | 2.7 | 4.4 | 6.9 | 11 | 18 | 28 | 35 |
| 30 A | 0.5 | 0.7 | 1.2 | 1.8 | 2.9 | 4.6 | 7.4 | 12 | 19 | 24 |
| 50 A | | 0.4 | 0.7 | 1.1 | 1.7 | 2.8 | 4.4 | 7.0 | 11 | 14 |
| 100 A | | | 0.3 | 0.5 | 0.9 | 1.4 | 2.2 | 3.5 | 5.6 | 7.0 |

- A blank cell means the wire is far too thin for that current.
- At 24 V the same wire runs twice as far; at 48 V four times as far.
- For 10% drop (acceptable for some resistive heaters, not for charging), multiply by about 3.3.
- For battery, charger and inverter cables aim for 1–2%: divide the lengths by 3 or 1.5.

Formula, if you need a size not shown: longest one-way run in metres = allowed drop in volts × 1,000 ÷ (2 × amps × ohms per km).

## Aluminium wire

Aluminium needs about 1.6 times the area of copper for the same resistance: go two AWG sizes thicker, or one or two metric sizes up. Use terminals rated for aluminium and keep the joints tight; aluminium creeps and oxidises, and loose joints overheat.

## Estimating unmarked wire

- Solid wire: measure the bare diameter and find the nearest row in table 1.
- Stranded wire: count the strands, measure one strand, and work out area = strands × 0.785 × diameter². Compare with the mm² column.
- Insulation thickness varies a lot: never judge wire by its outside size.
